Figure 1. Natural carboxyl polyether ionophores containing the ﬁve-membered hemiketal scaﬀold (HBFO) (highlighted in green). The underlined

figure_candidates.label: Figure 2
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 2. Proposed biosynthesis of lysocellin. a) Proposed biosynthesis sequence of the backbone of lysocellin. Each circle represents an enzymatic
domain: AT (acyl transferase), T (thiolation), KS (ketosynthase), DH (dehydratase), ER (enoyl reductase), KR (ketoreductase), and TE (thioesterase).
White circles indicate inactive domains. The stereochemistry of the lysocellin backbone is based on the stereochemistry of lysocellin.[35] b) Proposed
tailoring reactions of lysocellin. The order by which the cyclization reactions occur is unknown. All tailoring reactions are portrayed to occur on the
assembly line, though it is currently uncertain at which point the compound is released as the free acid.

figure_candidates.caption:

of S. longwoodensis. a) MS chromatograms from fermentations of S.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 4
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 4. NMR evaluation of lysocellin and pre-lysocellin. a) Structures of lysocellin and pre-lysocellin with numbered carbon atoms. HMBC and NOE
correlations can be found in Figure S12 and S13. b) Key diﬀerence observed between 1H (top) and 13C (bottom) NMR spectra of lysocellin and
pre-lysocellin. c) Diﬀerences in chemical shifts in the 1H (top) and 13C (bottom) NMR spectra of lysocellin and pre-lysocellin.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 5
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 5. Comparative biological data for lysocellin and pre-lysocellin. a) Representative dose-response curve demonstrating eﬀects on antibacterial
activity in S. aureus and cell viability in the mammalian cell line BJ. Points are mean ± SD, n = 3. b) Summary data of antibacterial MIC and MBC
(N = 2) and mammalian cell viability IC50 (N = 2). Data is mean over biological replicates. c) Cell painting assay with lysocellin. Left: Representative
cell painting images of DMSO, narasin, nanchangmycin, lysocellin, and pre-lysocellin. The bottom row of images represents vehicle control (DMSO)
and pre-lysocellin, which does not show mitochondrial perturbaton (red stain), compared to active ionophores in the top row of images. Scale
bar = 50 µm. Right: Heatmap of phenotypic ﬁngerprint of ionophores sorted by hierarchical clustering shows tight correlations between known
ionophores and lysocellin.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 6
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 6. Direct oxidation of pre-lysocellin to lysocellin by LyoI. a) HPLC-MS chromatograms (TIC) of the chemoenzymatic conversion of
pre-lysocellin to lysocellin using LyoI, ferredoxin/ferredoxin reductase, glucose-6-phosphate/glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogense and NADPH at
diﬀerent time points. b) Polyether ionophores containing unhydroxylated hydrobifuran moieties similar to the ones of pre-lysocellin.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 7
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 7. Investigation of conservation sequences in LyoI. a) Comparison of the conservation sequence A/G-G-X-D/E-T-T/S, which includes the
acid–alcohol pair (D/E-T), in LyoI with Streptomyces strains producing the polyether ionophores salinomycin, monensin, nanchangmycin, and
nigericin. b) Structural analysis of the proximity of T238 (green) and I237 (red) to the active site heme group in LyoI using AlphaFold 3.[56] c) The 10
(I-X) largest clusters along with LyoI’s cluster (LII) of the sequence similarity network (SSN) of LyoI. In the cases, where most enzymes of a speciﬁc
cluster are found in proximity to a speciﬁc type of BGC, this has been noted next to the cluster number. The full SNN can be found in Figure S9.
